questions.prompt: How does an entity differ from a value object?

options.text: An entity is immutable; a value object has identity
An entity has a persistent identity (compared by id); a value object has no identity and is compared by its attributes
An entity lives in the database; a value object lives in the UI

questions.explanation: Entities have identity that persists as attributes change (compared by id); value objects are usually immutable and compared by value.

questions.prompt: What is an 'anemic domain model,' and why is it often an anti-pattern?

options.text: Objects rich with behavior; it's ideal
Data-only objects (getters/setters) with all rules in separate services, so objects can go invalid and logic gets duplicated
A model with too few tables
A model that uses value objects

questions.explanation: When real rules exist, an anemic model (data-only objects + fat services) lets objects reach invalid states and scatters logic. A rich model keeps data and its rules together.

questions.prompt: A rule that must always hold for an object to be valid is called an ______, and the entity should protect its own.
questions.explanation: Entities enforce their invariants by validating on creation and only allowing safe changes, making invalid states unrepresentable.

questions.prompt: Which are true about Clean Architecture's 'Entities layer' vs DDD's 'Entity'? Select all that apply.

options.text: DDD's Entity is a specific kind of object (with identity)
Clean's Entities layer is a location holding all enterprise business rules
They are exactly the same term
Clean's Entities layer can include value objects and domain services

questions.explanation: DDD's Entity is one kind of object; Clean's Entities layer is a place holding enterprise rules, which may include DDD entities, value objects, and domain services. They overlap but aren't identical.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which an entity keeps itself valid.

items.text: Allow changes only through safe methods
Reject any change that would break an invariant

questions.explanation: Validate on creation, refuse to construct invalid objects, and gate all mutations so invariants always hold.

questions.prompt: Classify each as an Entity or a Value Object.
questions.explanation: Things with continuity/identity are entities; immutable things defined purely by their attributes are value objects.
